questions.question: The unit for permittivity of free space $(\varepsilon_0)$ is:
questions.answer:
**(C) $C^{2}N^{-1}m^{-2}$**

From $F=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^{2}}$,

$$\varepsilon_0=\frac{q_1q_2}{4\pi Fr^{2}}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{unit}=\frac{\text{C}^{2}}{\text{N}\,\text{m}^{2}}=\text{C}^{2}\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}$$

which is the same as F m$^{-1}$.

questions.question: In an electric circuit the algebraic sum of currents meeting at a point is:
questions.answer:
**(A) zero**

This is Kirchhoff's junction (point) rule:

$$\sum I=0$$

It is a statement of the conservation of charge — the charge entering a junction must equal the charge leaving it, since no charge can accumulate there.

questions.question: A wire carries a current of $1\ \mu$A. If charge on an electron is $1.5\times10^{-19}$ C, then number of electrons flowing per second through the wire is:
questions.answer:
**(A) $0.625\times10^{13}$**

The charge crossing the wire per second is

$$q=It=1\times10^{-6}\times1=10^{-6}\ \text{C}$$

The number of electrons is

$$n=\frac{q}{e}=\frac{10^{-6}}{1.6\times10^{-19}}=6.25\times10^{12}=0.625\times10^{13}$$

(The paper's own key, $0.625\times10^{13}$, uses $e=1.6\times10^{-19}$ C.)

questions.question: When an ammeter is shunted, its measuring range:
questions.answer:
**(B) increases**

A shunt is a small resistance $S$ connected in parallel with the ammeter coil of resistance $G$. It diverts most of the current, so a much larger total current can flow for the same full-scale deflection:

$$I=I_g\left(1+\frac{G}{S}\right)$$

Hence the range of the ammeter is increased by the factor $\left(1+\dfrac{G}{S}\right)$.

questions.topic: Magnetic Dipole in a Uniform Field
questions.question: A magnet of magnetic moment $\vec M$ is lying along a uniform magnetic field $\vec B$. The work done in rotating the magnet by $90^\circ$ is:
questions.answer:
**(C) $MB$**

The potential energy of a magnetic dipole is $U=-MB\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec M$ and $\vec B$. Initially $\theta_1=0^\circ$, finally $\theta_2=90^\circ$, so the work done is

$$W=U_2-U_1=-MB\cos90^\circ-(-MB\cos0^\circ)=0+MB=MB$$

*(Note: the printed answer key marks 2MB; that value would correspond to rotating the magnet through $180^\circ$, from $\theta=0$ to $\theta=180^\circ$, where $W=MB-(-MB)=2MB$. For a $90^\circ$ rotation the work done is MB, so the key appears to be an error.)*

questions.question: The ratio of root-mean-square value and peak value of alternating current is:
questions.answer:
**(A) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$**

For a sinusoidal current $I=I_0\sin\omega t$,

$$I_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_0^{T}I_0^{2}\sin^{2}\omega t\,dt}=\frac{I_0}{\sqrt2}$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{I_{\text{rms}}}{I_0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}=0.707$$

(The same ratio holds for voltage; the mean value over a half cycle is $\dfrac{2I_0}{\pi}$.)

questions.question: Speed of electromagnetic wave in free space is:
questions.answer:
**(C) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$**

Maxwell's equations give, for a plane electromagnetic wave in free space,

$$c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times8.85\times10^{-12}}}=3\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$

In a medium, $v=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}}=\dfrac{c}{n}$.

questions.question: When a ray of light passes from one medium to another, which of the following does not change?
questions.answer:
**(B) Frequency**

When light enters a new medium, its speed changes ($v=c/n$) and hence its wavelength changes ($\lambda_m=\lambda/n$); its direction changes, so the refractive index it experiences changes.

But the number of vibrations per second — the **frequency** — is fixed by the source and remains unchanged across the boundary. The energy of each photon, $h\nu$, is also unchanged.

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: Dimensions of Planck constant $(h)$ is:
questions.answer:
**(B) $ML^{2}T^{-1}$**

From $E=h\nu$, the unit of $h$ is J s, so

$$[h]=[\text{energy}][\text{time}]=ML^{2}T^{-2}\cdot T=ML^{2}T^{-1}$$

which is the same as the dimension of **angular momentum** — a useful check, since Bohr's quantisation condition sets $L=nh/2\pi$.

*(The printed key letter is (c), but the printed option (c) is $ML^{2}T^{-2}$ — the dimension of energy, not of $h$. The dimension of Planck's constant is $ML^{2}T^{-1}$, which is printed as option (b).)*

questions.question: Which of the following is not a fundamental particle?
questions.answer:
**(C) $\alpha$-particle**

An $\alpha$-particle is a helium nucleus, made of two protons and two neutrons — so it is a composite particle, not fundamental.

Neutrons, protons and electrons are all listed as fundamental particles in the school-level classification (strictly, the proton and neutron are themselves made of quarks, but the standard textbook list treats the electron, proton and neutron as the fundamental building blocks of matter).

questions.question: In an atom, electrons can revolve only in those orbits in which its angular momentum is integral multiple of:
questions.answer:
**(A) $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$**

Bohr's quantisation condition is

$$mvr=\frac{nh}{2\pi},\qquad n=1,2,3,\dots$$

so the angular momentum is an integral multiple of $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}=\hbar$. This is why angular momentum is naturally measured in units of $\hbar$.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: As temperature increases, the resistance of a semiconductor:
questions.answer:
**(B) decreases**

In a semiconductor the number of charge carriers increases exponentially with temperature:

$$n\propto T^{3/2}e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$$

This enormous increase in $n$ far outweighs the decrease in relaxation time, so the conductivity increases and the resistance decreases. Semiconductors therefore have a **negative temperature coefficient of resistance**, unlike metals.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: The Boolean expression for OR gate is:
questions.answer:
**(A) $A+B=Y$**

An OR gate gives a high output when **any** of its inputs is high, so its Boolean expression is

$$Y=A+B$$

*(Note: the printed answer key marks option (c) $\bar A\cdot\bar B=Y$. That is not the OR gate: by De Morgan's theorem $\overline{A+B}=\bar A\cdot\bar B$, so $\bar A\cdot\bar B$ is the complement of the OR output — it is the output of a NOR gate's first stage, and it equals $\overline{A+B}$, not $A+B$. The correct expression for an OR gate is $A+B=Y$, option (a), which is what is given here.)*

questions.question: Radio waves are reflected from:
questions.answer:
**(A) Ionosphere**

In the upper atmosphere (roughly 80–400 km) solar radiation ionises the air, creating the ionosphere — layers of free electrons and ions. Radio waves of frequency up to about 30 MHz are reflected back towards the earth by these layers, which is what makes long-distance short-wave communication possible.

The stratosphere and troposphere do not contain enough ionisation to reflect radio waves.

questions.question: Coaxial cable has a band width of:
questions.answer:
**(C) 750 MHz**

A coaxial (co-ax) cable consists of a central copper conductor surrounded by an insulating sheath, a braided metallic shield and an outer jacket. Because the outer conductor shields the signal from external interference, it can carry high-frequency signals over moderate distances, and its bandwidth is of the order of

$$\text{bandwidth}\approx750\ \text{MHz}$$

(Compared with a twisted pair, whose bandwidth is only a few MHz.)

questions.question: What are electric field lines? Mention two of its properties.
questions.answer:
**Electric field lines** are curved or straight imaginary lines in an electric field such that the tangent drawn at any point on them gives the direction of the electric field at that point. The number of lines per unit area (perpendicular to the lines) is proportional to the magnitude of the field.

**Properties (any two):**

1. Electric field lines begin on positive charge and end on negative charge (or go to/come from infinity); they do not form closed loops.
2. Two electric field lines never cross each other — if they did, the field at the crossing point would have two directions at once.

Other properties: they are always perpendicular to the surface of a conductor; they are continuous curves in a charge-free region; they contract longitudinally for attraction between unlike charges and exert lateral pressure for repulsion between like charges.

questions.question: Define emf of a cell. Mention two differences between emf and terminal potential difference.
questions.answer:
**Emf of a cell** is defined as the potential difference between its terminals when **no current** is drawn from it (open circuit). Equivalently, it is the work done by the cell in carrying unit positive charge once round the complete circuit, $\varepsilon=W/q$.

**Differences between emf and terminal potential difference:**

| E.M.F. | Terminal Potential Difference |
|---|---|
| The potential difference between the terminals when no current is drawn from the cell. | The potential difference between the terminals in a closed circuit, i.e. when current is drawn from the cell. |
| The term e.m.f. is reserved for the potential difference of the source itself; it is a property of the cell. | The term potential difference is used for the voltage measured between any two points of an electric circuit. |
| It is independent of the external circuit (fixed for a given cell). | It depends on the current drawn: $V=\varepsilon-Ir$. |

questions.question: Define critical angle. Mention the conditions for total internal reflection of light.
questions.answer:
**Critical angle ($C$):** When a ray of light passes from a denser medium into a rarer medium, the angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction becomes $90^\circ$ is called the critical angle. It is given by

$$\sin C=\frac{n_r}{n_d}=\frac{1}{n}$$

**Conditions for total internal reflection:**

1. The light must travel from a **denser medium to a rarer medium** (e.g. from glass or water to air).
2. The angle of incidence in the denser medium must be **greater than the critical angle** for the pair of media ($i>C$).

When both conditions hold, no light is refracted and the entire beam is reflected back into the denser medium — total internal reflection. (Examples: sparkling of diamond, mirage, light pipe, totally reflecting prisms.)

questions.question: What are microwaves? Mention two of its applications.
questions.answer:
**Microwaves** are electromagnetic waves whose wavelengths range from about $0.1$ m to $1$ mm, corresponding to frequencies of about $10^{9}$ Hz to $3\times10^{11}$ Hz. They lie between the radio waves and the infrared region of the electromagnetic spectrum, and are produced by oscillating electrons in a cavity — commonly by Klystron, Magnetron and Gunn diode oscillators.

**Applications:**

1. Microwaves are used in radar systems for aircraft navigation, air-traffic control and speed measurement.
2. They are used in microwave ovens for cooking and warming food (the microwaves are absorbed by water molecules, whose vibration heats the food).

They are also used for satellite and cellular-phone communication and for atomic and molecular research.

questions.question: Define coefficient of self induction and coefficient of mutual induction.
questions.answer:
**Coefficient of self induction ($L$):** The coefficient of self induction of a coil is the magnetic flux linked with the coil when a unit current flows through it:

$$L=\frac{\Phi}{I}$$

Equivalently, it is numerically equal to the emf induced in the coil when the rate of change of current in it is $1$ A s$^{-1}$:

$$\varepsilon=-L\frac{dI}{dt}$$

Its SI unit is the henry (H).

**Coefficient of mutual induction ($M$):** The coefficient of mutual induction of a pair of coils is the magnetic flux linked with one coil when a unit current passes through the other coil:

$$M=\frac{\Phi_2}{I_1}=\frac{\Phi_1}{I_2}$$

Equivalently, it is numerically equal to the emf induced in one coil when the current in the other changes at the rate of $1$ A s$^{-1}$:

$$\varepsilon_2=-M\frac{dI_1}{dt}$$

Its SI unit is also the henry (H).

questions.question: What is Rutherford's nuclear model of atom?
questions.answer:
**Rutherford's nuclear model** (proposed in 1911 on the basis of the $\alpha$-particle scattering experiment):

1. The entire positive charge and almost the whole mass of the atom is concentrated in a very small central core called the **nucleus** ($\sim10^{-15}$ m, compared with the atom's $\sim10^{-10}$ m).
2. The nucleus is surrounded by a suitable number of **electrons**, so that the atom as a whole is electrically neutral. Most of the atom is empty space.
3. The electrons revolve round the nucleus in various orbits; the necessary centripetal force is provided by the electrostatic force of attraction between the electrons and the nucleus:

$$\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Ze^{2}}{r^{2}}=\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$$

This model explained the large-angle scattering of $\alpha$-particles, but it could not explain the stability of the atom or its discrete line spectra.

questions.question: Define mass defect and nuclear binding energy.
questions.answer:
**Mass defect ($\Delta M$):** The difference between the sum of the masses of the protons and neutrons that make up a nucleus and the mass of the nucleus itself:

$$\Delta M=[Zm_p+(A-Z)m_n]-M_{\text{nucleus}}$$

where $m_p$ is the mass of a proton, $m_n$ that of a neutron and $M_{\text{nucleus}}$ the mass of the nucleus. It is measured in a.m.u. (or kg).

**Nuclear binding energy ($E_b$):** The total energy required to disintegrate a nucleus into its constituent protons and neutrons is called the binding energy of the nucleus:

$$E_b=\Delta M\,c^{2}$$

It is measured in MeV ($1$ u $\equiv931.5$ MeV). Binding energy per nucleon $E_b/A$ measures the stability of the nucleus.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: Why is the base region of a transistor thin and lightly doped? Explain.
questions.answer:
The base region of a transistor separates the emitter and the collector, and its thickness and doping control how much of the emitter current reaches the collector.

- The **emitter** is heavily doped so that it supplies a large number of majority carriers into the base.
- The **collector** is moderately doped and physically larger, to collect the carriers.

**Reason for a thin and lightly doped base:**

1. **Thin base:** The majority carriers injected from the emitter into the base travel by diffusion across the base to the collector. If the base were thick, the carriers would spend a long time in the base and most of them would recombine with the oppositely charged carriers there before reaching the collector. Because the base is made very thin ($\sim10^{-6}$ m), the transit time is short, so most of the injected carriers reach the collector. Hence the collector current remains almost equal to the emitter current and the current gain is large.
2. **Lightly doped base:** If the base were heavily doped, its own majority carriers would be numerous and the injected minority carriers would recombine with them in large numbers; also the base would draw a large current of its own. Light doping keeps the recombination in the base small, so a very small base current controls a large collector current ($\alpha=I_C/I_E\approx0.95$–$0.99$).

Thus, the thin, lightly doped base ensures that the output (collector) current is only slightly less than the input (emitter) current, giving good current gain and large output. If the base were thick and heavily doped, most carriers would be lost by recombination and the collector current would be reduced considerably.

questions.question: Explain the principle of a potentiometer. Draw the circuit diagram for the comparison of emf of two primary cells using a potentiometer.
questions.answer:
**Principle of a potentiometer:** It works on the principle that the potential difference across any part of a uniform wire is directly proportional to the length of that part, when a constant current flows through the wire.

$$V\propto l\ \Rightarrow\ V=kl,\qquad k=\frac{V}{L}\ \text{(potential gradient)}$$

This is because a uniform wire has the same resistance per unit length, so $V=IR=\left(I\cdot\dfrac{\rho}{A}\right)l$.

**Comparison of the emfs of two cells:**

A battery (driver cell), a rheostat, a key $K$ and the potentiometer wire $AB$ form the primary circuit. The two cells whose emfs $\varepsilon_1$ and $\varepsilon_2$ are to be compared are connected through a two-way key to the galvanometer, which is joined to the jockey $J$ on the wire.

**Working:**

1. Insert the first cell in the circuit and find the balance point $J_1$ where the galvanometer shows no deflection, at length $l_1$:

$$\varepsilon_1=kl_1$$

2. Replace it by the second cell and find the new balance length $l_2$:

$$\varepsilon_2=kl_2$$

3. Dividing,

$$\boxed{\frac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2}=\frac{l_1}{l_2}}$$

Thus the ratio of the emfs is equal to the ratio of the balancing lengths. Since no current is drawn from the cell at balance, the potentiometer measures the true emf, not the terminal voltage.

questions.topic: Magnetic Dipole Moment of an Orbital Electron
questions.question: Derive an expression for the magnetic dipole moment of orbital electron of an atom.
questions.answer:
In an atom the electron revolves round the nucleus in a circular orbit. This revolving electron is equivalent to a tiny current loop, and hence behaves as a magnetic dipole.

**Step 1 — Equivalent current.** If the electron of charge $e$ revolves with speed $v$ in an orbit of radius $r$, the time period is

$$T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}$$

The equivalent current (charge flowing per unit time) is

$$I=\frac{e}{T}=\frac{ev}{2\pi r}$$

**Step 2 — Magnetic moment.** For a current loop of area $A=\pi r^{2}$,

$$\mu_l=IA=\frac{ev}{2\pi r}\times\pi r^{2}=\frac{evr}{2}$$

**Step 3 — In terms of the angular momentum.** For a circular orbit the orbital angular momentum is $L=m_evr$, so $vr=\dfrac{L}{m_e}$. Hence

$$\boxed{\mu_l=\frac{e}{2m_e}L}$$

In vector form, since the current flows opposite to the electron's motion,

$$\vec\mu_l=-\frac{e}{2m_e}\vec L$$

The ratio

$$\frac{\mu_l}{L}=\frac{e}{2m_e}=\frac{1.6\times10^{-19}}{2\times9.11\times10^{-31}}=8.8\times10^{10}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}$$

is called the **gyromagnetic ratio**; it is the same for all orbital electrons, which is the basis of the Bohr magneton $\mu_B=\dfrac{eh}{4\pi m_e}$.

questions.topic: Magnetic Field at the Centre of a Coil
questions.question: A circular coil of wire consisting of 100 turns, each of radius 8.0 cm, carries a current of 0.40 A. What is the magnitude of magnetic field at the centre of the coil?
questions.answer:
Given: $N=100$, $r=8.0$ cm $=0.08$ m, $I=0.40$ A.

The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of $N$ turns is

$$B=\frac{\mu_0NI}{2r}$$

Substituting,

$$B=\frac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times100\times0.40}{2\times0.08}$$

$$B=\frac{4\times3.14\times10^{-7}\times40}{0.16}$$

$$B=\frac{5.03\times10^{-5}}{0.16}$$

$$\boxed{B\approx3.14\times10^{-4}\ \text{T}}$$

**Answer:** The magnetic field at the centre is about $3.14\times10^{-4}$ T ($3.14$ gauss), directed along the axis of the coil.

questions.question: What is polarisation of light? State and explain Brewster's law.
questions.answer:
**Polarisation of light:** During the propagation of a light wave, the particles of the medium vibrate about their mean positions in all directions in the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation. If the vibrations are restricted to take place (mainly) in one particular direction, the light is said to be **polarised** (plane polarised). This shows that light is a transverse wave.

**Brewster's law:** The refractive index of a refracting medium is numerically equal to the tangent of the polarising angle (the angle of incidence at which the reflected light is completely polarised):

$$\mu=\tan\theta_p$$

where $\theta_p$ is the polarising (Brewster) angle.

**Explanation:** When unpolarised light is incident on a transparent medium at the polarising angle, the reflected and the refracted rays are perpendicular to each other:

$$\theta_p+r=90^\circ$$

By Snell's law,

$$\mu=\frac{\sin\theta_p}{\sin r}=\frac{\sin\theta_p}{\sin(90^\circ-\theta_p)}=\frac{\sin\theta_p}{\cos\theta_p}=\tan\theta_p$$

which is Brewster's law. At this angle the reflected ray is completely plane polarised (with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence), while the refracted ray is only partially polarised. For glass, $\mu=1.5$ gives $\theta_p=56.3^\circ$.

questions.question: In Young's experiment, the slits are 0.03 cm apart and screen is 1.5 m away from the surface of the slits. The distance between the central fringe and the fourth bright fringe is 1 cm. Find the wavelength of light used.
questions.answer:
Given:

$$d=0.03\ \text{cm}=3\times10^{-4}\ \text{m},\quad D=1.5\ \text{m},\quad n=4,\quad y=1\ \text{cm}=1\times10^{-2}\ \text{m}$$

The distance of the $n$th bright fringe from the central maximum is

$$y=\frac{n\lambda D}{d}$$

Rearranging for $\lambda$:

$$\lambda=\frac{yd}{nD}=\frac{1\times10^{-2}\times3\times10^{-4}}{4\times1.5}$$

$$\lambda=\frac{3\times10^{-6}}{6}=0.5\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$$

$$\boxed{\lambda=5\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}=5000\ \text{Å}}$$

**Answer:** The wavelength of the light used is $5\times10^{-7}$ m, i.e. $5000$ Å (green light).

questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: What is photoelectric effect? Establish Einstein's equation for photoelectric effect.
questions.answer:
**Photoelectric effect:** The phenomenon of emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of suitable (sufficiently high) frequency falls on it is called photoelectric effect (first observed by Hertz in 1887, explained by Einstein in 1905). The emitted electrons are called photoelectrons and the effect is practically instantaneous.

**Einstein's explanation:** Einstein treated light as a stream of photons, each of energy $h\nu$, and applied the law of conservation of energy. When a photon is absorbed by an electron of the metal, its energy is used up in two ways:

1. In ejecting the electron from the metal surface — this needs a minimum energy equal to the work function $W_0=h\nu_0$, where $\nu_0$ is the threshold frequency.
2. In giving kinetic energy to the emitted electron.

Hence, for the most energetic electron,

$$h\nu=W_0+K_{\max}$$

$$\boxed{h\nu=h\nu_0+\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}_{\max}}$$

or, in terms of stopping potential $V_0$ ($K_{\max}=eV_0$),

$$eV_0=h(\nu-\nu_0)$$

**Consequences:**

- If $\nu<\nu_0$, the energy of a photon is insufficient and no emission occurs, however intense the light.
- $K_{\max}$ increases linearly with $\nu$ but is independent of the intensity.
- The number of photoelectrons (and hence the photocurrent) is proportional to the intensity, because intensity fixes the number of photons.

These features could not be explained by the wave theory, so the effect establishes the particle (photon) nature of light.

questions.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
questions.question: What is Zener diode? Explain its action as a voltage regulator.
questions.answer:
**Zener diode:** A Zener diode is a specially designed junction diode (heavily doped) which can operate in the region of reverse breakdown voltage without being damaged. In reverse bias, beyond the Zener voltage $V_Z$, its current increases very rapidly while the voltage across it stays almost constant. It is used for providing a constant voltage supply.

**Action as a voltage regulator:**

In the circuit, the input d.c. voltage $V_{in}$ (whose variations are to be regulated) is applied through a series resistance $R$. The Zener diode is connected in reverse bias across $V_{in}$, and the load resistance $R_L$ across which a constant voltage is required is connected in parallel with the diode.

The total current $I$ passing through $R$ equals the sum of the diode current and the load current:

$$I=I_Z+I_L,\qquad V_{in}=IR+V_Z,\qquad V_{out}=V_Z$$

- **When the input voltage increases**, the extra voltage is dropped across $R$ and the Zener current $I_Z$ increases, while the voltage across the diode — and hence across the load — stays fixed at $V_Z$.
- **When the load current increases** (load resistance falls), $I_Z$ decreases by the same amount, keeping $I$ and hence the drop $IR$ unchanged, so $V_{out}$ stays at $V_Z$.

Thus the output voltage remains constant at the Zener breakdown voltage, and the series resistance absorbs the excess voltage. This is voltage regulation.

questions.question: What is modulation? Why is modulation needed?
questions.answer:
**Modulation** is the process of superimposing the audio-frequency (message) signal over a high-frequency carrier wave so that the message can be transmitted over long distances. The message signal modulates some characteristic (amplitude, frequency or phase) of the carrier.

**Need (necessity) of modulation:**

1. **To reduce the height (size) of the transmitting antenna:** For efficient radiation the antenna height should be at least $\lambda/4$. For an audio frequency of $20$ kHz, $\lambda=15$ km and the antenna would have to be about $3.75$ km high — impractical. With a carrier of, say, $1$ MHz, $\lambda=300$ m and a $75$ m antenna suffices. Modulation raises the frequency and hence shortens the required antenna.
2. **To increase the effective power radiated by the antenna:** The power radiated by an antenna is proportional to $\left(\dfrac{l}{\lambda}\right)^{2}$, so a high frequency (short wavelength) gives far greater radiated power for the same antenna length.
3. **To avoid mixing up (interference) of signals from different transmitters:** If many stations transmitted the same base-band audio frequencies, their signals would overlap and could not be separated. Each station is therefore allotted a different carrier frequency, and the receiver can be tuned to select only that carrier.
4. **To accommodate the available bandwidth and to superimpose the low-frequency message onto a high frequency** for efficient transmission through the channel.

questions.topic: Electric Potential due to a Dipole
questions.question: Define electric potential. Derive an expression for electric potential at any point due to an electric dipole.
questions.answer:
**Electric potential:** The electric potential at a point is defined as the amount of work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point (without acceleration). For a point charge $q$,

$$V=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r}$$

**Potential at any point due to a dipole:**

Consider an electric dipole of charges $+q$ and $-q$ separated by distance $2l$, with centre $O$. Let $P$ be a point at distance $r$ from $O$, with $OP$ making an angle $\theta$ with the dipole axis. Let $r_1$ and $r_2$ be the distances of $P$ from $-q$ and $+q$ respectively.

**Step 1 — Superposition.** The potential at $P$ is the algebraic sum of the potentials due to the two charges:

$$V=V_1+V_2=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{(-q)}{r_1}+\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r_2}$$

$$V=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{r_2}-\frac{1}{r_1}\right]\quad\text{... (i)}$$

**Step 2 — Distances to first order in $l$.** Dropping perpendiculars from the charges onto $OP$, for $r\gg l$:

$$r_1\approx r+l\cos\theta,\qquad r_2\approx r-l\cos\theta$$

**Step 3 — Substitute:**

$$V=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{r-l\cos\theta}-\frac{1}{r+l\cos\theta}\right]=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\frac{2l\cos\theta}{r^{2}-l^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}$$

**Step 4 — Dipole approximation ($r\gg l$):** neglect $l^{2}\cos^{2}\theta$ compared with $r^{2}$, and use $p=q(2l)$:

$$\boxed{V=\frac{p\cos\theta}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^{2}}=\frac{\vec p\cdot\hat r}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^{2}}}$$

**Special cases:**

- **Axial point** ($\theta=0^\circ$): $V=\dfrac{p}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^{2}}=2\times$ the value due to a single charge.
- **Equatorial point** ($\theta=90^\circ$): $\cos90^\circ=0$, so $V=0$ — the potential is zero everywhere on the equatorial line of the dipole.

questions.question: State Gauss's theorem in electrostatics. Use this theorem to derive expressions for electric field due to uniformly charged thin spherical shell at a point (i) outside and, (ii) inside the shell.
questions.answer:
**Gauss's theorem:** The total electric flux passing through a closed surface equals $1/\varepsilon_0$ times the net charge enclosed within that surface:

$$\phi=\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec S=\frac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$$

Consider a uniformly charged thin spherical shell (hollow sphere) of radius $R$ carrying total charge $+q$, with centre $O$.

**(i) Field at a point outside the shell ($r>R$):**

Let $P$ be a point at distance $r>R$ from $O$. Draw a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ through $P$. At every point of this surface the field is radial and has the same magnitude, and the angle between $\vec E$ and $d\vec S$ is $0^\circ$.

$$\phi=\oint E\,dS\cos0^\circ=E\oint dS=E\,(4\pi r^{2})\quad\text{... (1)}$$

By Gauss's theorem (the whole charge $q$ is enclosed):

$$\phi=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}q\quad\text{... (2)}$$

Equating (1) and (2):

$$E\,(4\pi r^{2})=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{E=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q}{r^{2}}}$$

In vector form, $\vec E=\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}}\hat r$. Outside, the shell behaves as though all its charge were concentrated at its centre.

**(ii) Field at a point inside the shell ($r<R$):**

Now take $P$ inside the shell at distance $r<R$ and draw the concentric Gaussian surface through it. This surface encloses **no charge** ($q_{\text{enclosed}}=0$), so by Gauss's theorem

$$\phi=E\,(4\pi r^{2})=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}\times0=0$$

$$\boxed{E=0}$$

Hence the electric field at every point inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell is zero. The potential inside, however, is constant and equal to $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{R}$ (the same as on the surface).

questions.question: State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction. Derive expression for emf induced in a coil rotating uniformly in a uniform magnetic field. Mention the nature of this emf.
questions.answer:
**Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction:**

**First law:** Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a conductor (circuit) changes, an emf is induced in it.

**Second law:** The magnitude of the induced emf is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the conductor (and to the number of turns):

$$e=-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$$

**Emf induced in a coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field:**

Let a coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ be placed in a uniform magnetic field $B$, and let it rotate with uniform angular velocity $\omega$ about an axis perpendicular to the field. If initially ($t=0$) the normal to the coil is along the field, then at time $t$ the angle between the normal and the field is

$$\theta=\omega t$$

The magnetic flux linked with the coil at that instant is

$$\Phi=NBA\cos\theta=NBA\cos\omega t$$

By Faraday's law,

$$e=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}=-\frac{d}{dt}(NBA\cos\omega t)$$

$$e=-NBA\frac{d}{dt}(\cos\omega t)=-NBA(-\omega\sin\omega t)$$

$$\boxed{e=NBA\omega\sin\omega t=E_0\sin\omega t},\qquad E_0=NBA\omega$$

**Nature of the emf:** The induced emf varies periodically (sinusoidally) with time, both in magnitude and in direction — it is an **alternating emf**. Its maximum value $E_0=NBA\omega$ occurs when $\theta=\omega t=90^\circ$ (the plane of the coil parallel to the field) and it is zero when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. This is the principle of the a.c. generator.

questions.question: Derive expression for instantaneous current in a series L-C-R circuit if connected to an alternating emf. Obtain the condition for resonance.
questions.answer:
In a series LCR circuit the same current $I$ flows through $L$, $C$ and $R$, and the applied voltage is the phasor sum of the three voltages. Let

$$V=V_0\sin\omega t$$

The voltage across the inductor leads the current by $90^\circ$, that across the capacitor lags by $90^\circ$, and that across the resistor is in phase with the current. Hence

$$V=\sqrt{V_R^{2}+(V_L-V_C)^{2}}=I\sqrt{R^{2}+(X_L-X_C)^{2}}=IZ$$

where the impedance is

$$Z=\sqrt{R^{2}+(X_L-X_C)^{2}}=\sqrt{R^{2}+\left(\omega L-\frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^{2}}$$

and the phase angle by which the voltage leads the current is

$$\tan\phi=\frac{X_L-X_C}{R}=\frac{\omega L-\dfrac{1}{\omega C}}{R}$$

**Current:**

$$I=\frac{V}{Z}=\frac{V_0}{Z}\sin(\omega t-\phi)=I_0\sin(\omega t-\phi)$$

$$\boxed{I_0=\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{R^{2}+\left(\omega L-\frac{1}{\omega C}\right)^{2}}}}$$

**Condition for resonance:** The current is maximum when the impedance is minimum, i.e. when the reactances cancel:

$$X_L=X_C\ \Rightarrow\ \omega L=\frac{1}{\omega C}\ \Rightarrow\ \omega^{2}=\frac{1}{LC}$$

$$\boxed{\omega_r=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}},\qquad f_r=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}}$$

At resonance $Z=R$ (minimum), the current is maximum $I_0=V_0/R$, the phase angle is zero (the circuit behaves as purely resistive, voltage and current in phase), and the voltage across $L$ and $C$ may individually be much larger than the applied voltage (voltage magnification).

questions.question: For refraction at any spherical surface, establish the relation $\dfrac{n_2}{v}-\dfrac{n_1}{u}=\dfrac{n_2-n_1}{R}$, where terms have usual meanings.
questions.answer:
Consider a convex spherical refracting surface of radius of curvature $R$, separating a rarer medium of refractive index $n_1$ from a denser medium of refractive index $n_2$ ($n_2>n_1$). Let a point object $O$ lie on the principal axis at a distance $u$ from the pole $P$.

A ray from $O$ strikes the surface at $A$; $AN$ is the normal at $A$ (passing through the centre of curvature $C$). After refraction the ray bends towards the normal and meets the axis at $I$, the real image, at distance $v$.

**Step 1 — Relation between the angles.** Let $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ be the angles made by the incident ray, refracted ray and the normal respectively with the principal axis, and $i$, $r$ the angles of incidence and refraction at $A$.

From $\triangle AOC$ (exterior angle): $i=\alpha+\gamma$ ... (i)

From $\triangle AIC$ (exterior angle): $\gamma=r+\beta$ or $r=\gamma-\beta$ ... (ii)

**Step 2 — Small-angle approximation.** For paraxial rays the angles are small, so

$$\alpha\approx\frac{AN}{PO},\qquad \gamma\approx\frac{AN}{PC},\qquad \beta\approx\frac{AN}{PI}$$

$$i=\frac{AN}{PO}+\frac{AN}{PC},\qquad r=\frac{AN}{PC}-\frac{AN}{PI}$$

For a small aperture the point $N$ lies very close to $P$, so $PO\approx u$, $PI\approx v$, $PC\approx R$.

**Step 3 — Snell's law.** For small angles,

$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{n_2}{n_1}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{i}{r}=\frac{n_2}{n_1}\ \Rightarrow\ n_1i=n_2r$$

**Step 4 — Substitute:**

$$n_1\left(\frac{AN}{u}+\frac{AN}{R}\right)=n_2\left(\frac{AN}{R}-\frac{AN}{v}\right)$$

Cancelling $AN$:

$$\frac{n_1}{u}+\frac{n_1}{R}=\frac{n_2}{R}-\frac{n_2}{v}$$

**Step 5 — Apply the sign convention** (all distances measured from the pole, against the incident light being negative): $PO=-u$, $PI=+v$, $PC=+R$. Then

$$\frac{n_1}{-u}+\frac{n_1}{R}=\frac{n_2}{R}-\frac{n_2}{v}$$

$$\frac{n_2}{v}-\frac{n_1}{u}=\frac{n_2-n_1}{R}$$

which is the required relation.

questions.question: State Huygens' principle. Establish the law of refraction of light using Huygens' principle.
questions.answer:
**Huygens' principle:**

1. Every source of light is a centre of disturbance from which waves spread in all directions; the locus of all particles equidistant from the source is called a wavefront.
2. Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of new disturbance which produces secondary wavelets; these wavelets are spherical and travel with the speed of light in all directions in that medium.
3. The forward envelope (the common tangent) enclosing the secondary wavelets at any instant gives the new position of the wavefront at that instant.

**Law of refraction using Huygens' principle:**

Let $AB$ be a plane wavefront incident on the boundary $XY$ separating a rarer medium 1 (refractive index $n_1$, speed $v_1$) from a denser medium 2 (refractive index $n_2$, speed $v_2$, with $n_2>n_1$). Let $A$ touch the boundary at time $t=0$; in time $t$ the disturbance at $B$ travels to $C$ in medium 1, so

$$BC=v_1t$$

During the same interval, the secondary wavelets from $A$ travel in medium 2 a distance

$$AD=v_2t$$

Draw the tangent $CD$ from $C$ to the sphere of radius $AD$ centred at $A$; $CD$ is the refracted wavefront. The time taken by the wavelets to travel from $P$ to $R$ the same way must be the same for all points of the wavefront, which gives the condition $\dfrac{\sin i}{v_1}=\dfrac{\sin r}{v_2}$.

In the right triangles $ABC$ and $ADC$:

$$\sin i=\frac{BC}{AC}=\frac{v_1t}{AC},\qquad \sin r=\frac{AD}{AC}=\frac{v_2t}{AC}$$

Dividing,

$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{v_1}{v_2}$$

Multiplying and dividing the right-hand side by $c$, the speed of light in vacuum:

$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r}=\frac{c/v_2}{c/v_1}=\frac{n_2}{n_1}$$

$$\boxed{n_1\sin i=n_2\sin r}$$

which is **Snell's law of refraction**. The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
